evidence.section_title: Gillian Murphy, BA, MA, RMN, PGDE
evidence.quote: University of Western Sydney, Student Support Services, Penrith, Australia
University of Technology—Sydney, Faculty of Health, Sydney, Australia

Relatively little is known about the experiences of those bereaved by suicide, particularly in the weeks leading to the death of a loved one. This study used a qualitative methodology to explore the perspectives of close survivors of a completed suicide. Ten people who were bereaved by suicide participated in face-toface interviews

Further, all participants had to have experienced a completed suicide of a family member at least 12 months prior to being interviewed and had to have had dealings with official agencies (e.g., police, coroner, insurance company, funeral directors, banks) related to the suicide of a family member.

[/page/3/Text/10] Ten participants, 25–65 years of age, were recruited into this study. All had been in very close familial relationships with the deceased persons and were bereaved for between 2 and 20 years (see Table 1). All decedents were male, 20–60 years of age, and hanging was the most common form of suicide (n = 6).
Ten people who were bereaved by suicide participated in face-toface interviews that were digitally recorded, transcribed verbatim, and thematically analysed.
Interviews were used to collect narrative data to explore the experiences of individuals bereaved by suicide.

In order to be eligible to participate in this study, participants needed to be aged 18 years and over and fluent in the English language. Further, all participants had to have experienced a completed suicide of a family member at least 12 months prior to being interviewed and had to have had dealings with official agencies (e.g., police, coroner, insurance company, funeral directors, banks) related to the suicide of a family member.

[012_recruitment/page/2/Text/10] Participants self-selected after a media release advertising the study invited interested people to contact the researchers for further information. During initial contact, potential participants were asked a series of questions to ensure they fulfilled inclusion criteria. Once eligibility to participate was determined, the researchers sent out participant information sheets to interested individuals, explaining in detail what participation in the study would involve.

Face-to-face interviews with participants were conducted by two members of the research team (KP and GM) who have qualifications and extensive experience in mental health nursing and in interviewing vulnerable populations.

Data analysis was undertaken by all authors. As recommended by Braun and Clarke (2006), the researchers initially listened to audio recordings while reading the transcripts to ensure accuracy of the content and understanding of the context of the participants' narrative. Following this step, the researchers extensively engaged in the data independently by reading and re-reading transcripts. Data were then coded, grouped into categories, and over-arching themes after which all members of the research team compared and discussed their individual findings until agreement was attained.

A reflexive approach was applied throughout the research process to ensure the rigor of the study and its findings. That is, the researchers continually reflected on their own preconceptions and impressions and contemplated how these may influence the quality and interpretation of the data collected. Further enhancing the rigor of the study, credibility was achieved by all members of the research team independently analysing the data and discussing individual findings until consensus was reached (Polit & Beck, 2010).

[/page/3/Text/7] Several participants became emotional during their interviews. When this occurred, the interview was stopped and the participant was given the option to withdraw from the study and reminded of the availability of counselling services.

evidence.section_title: He Tried to Hang Himself: Purposeful Indications of Intent to End Life
evidence.quote: Noelene, in describing the suicide of her husband, recalled an event 3-weeks prior to his death that had been her first awareness of any sort of mental health problems.

evidence.section_title: They Sill Ignored It: Disappointment with Health Services
evidence.quote: I could see him getting worse and worse, but every time he went to hospital after he'd tried to stab himself or do something stupid, they let him out again because when he was in there, he looked like there was nothing wrong with him. He was the sort of person who could make himself look like there was nothing wrong with him and pretend and, to me, that was ridiculous. That this is a psychiatrist who supposedly knows—I even wrote in point form, all the weird things that he'd done when he was at home and all the things that he'd said and presented it to them and they still ignored it. (Kirsten).

[/page/6/Text/8] However, what became clear throughout this study was that many of the participants had indeed identified that their loved ones were at risk of suicide but were unable to procure the assistance they felt necessary to prevent their deaths. [/page/6/Text/11] Participants of this current study often perceived that health professionals were unhelpful and the lack of assistance provided was generally blamed on the health professionals' expressed need to maintain patient confidentiality.

Analysis revealed the following three themes: He Tried to Hang Himself: Purposeful indications of the intent to end life; They Still Ignored It: Disappointment with health services; and Nobody Talked to Me: Exclusion of family members from treatment information. Prior to the suicide of their loved one, participants had identified that the loved one was at risk and perceived they were unable to acquire appropriate assistance from services. Rather, services were perceived by participants as unsupportive and inadequate.

[/page/3/Text/13] one of the participants reported that the decedents had a prior history of mental health or substance abuse issues (see Table 2). [/page/3/Text/14] Although many had moved on in the sense that they were re-partnered, and able to function well in various aspects of their lives, all still experienced a deep sense of loss and continued to express their grief, sadness, and regret over the events surrounding the suicides. Their desire to contribute something positive was such that several participants were actively engaged in volunteer and activism works in the area of suicide bereavement and mental health support. Furthermore, a number of participants indicated that they considered their participation in this study to be a way that they could help others through sharing their experiences. [/page/3/Text/15] Thematic analysis revealed three key themes. These are: (1) He Tried to Hang Himself: Purposeful indications of the intent to end life; (2) They Still Ignored It: Disappointment with health services; and (3) Nobody Talked to Me: Exclusion of family members from treatment information.

[/page/6/Text/8] Most prominently, health services were perceived by participants as unsupportive and inadequate. This included the specialised mental health services. [/page/6/Text/12] It is acknowledged in previous literature that survivors of suicide receive considerably less support than people bereaved by other means (Faberow, Gallagher-Thompson, Gilewski, & Thompson, 1992). This is significant given that those bereaved by suicide are at a substantially higher risk of suicide themselves (Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2008; Department of Health, 2010; Krysinska, 2003). [/page/7/Text/2] Yet, suicide survivors were noted to state that the reasons for their involvement in research studies regarding suicide bereavement were to vent, gain insight into their own experiences, and have contact with a mental health professional. Essentially, they are seeking suitable forums for communications about their experiences (Dyregrov et al., 2010), which they have found difficult to access.
